newsitem.title: UK: Knee-jerk gilts dip but seen stoic under Labour.
newsitem.headline: Knee-jerk gilts dip but seen stoic under Labour.

text.p: British government bonds sagged under the weight of profit-taking in the early hours of Friday as Britain's Labour party sprinted to election victory and dealers expected further limited losses when the futures market opened.

But with a prudent interest rate rise on the cards, maybe even within the week, and a belief new Labour will be keen to establish its credentials in the financial markets, gilts look pretty rosy medium term, they added.

"If people are still long immediately tomorrow (Friday), we could lose a bit more, but further out, people will return to the focus that the Labour Party looks good for the markets," said Steve Scott, gilts analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.

The 10-year benchmark rose to around 99-07 late on Thursday night from 98-27 after initial exit polls predicted a landslide majority for the Labour Party. But as the results came in so did the profit takers, who pushed the paper down to 98-18 for a yield of 7.44 percent.
"We might take out a bit of the very loose money (Friday)...people who were holding gilts up to the election," said Scott.
"But anyone looking longer than the immediate term I expect to be happy to sit with it and medium term the market should do quite well."
British gilts, partly due to the country's tortuous indecision on European monetary union, are among the highest yielding government bond markets in Europe.
Analysts said the prospect of U.S. non-farm payrolls, due at 1230 GMT, would dampen trade and give investors an excuse to hold fire.

They said the monster majority which it appeared Labour was securing may ring alarm bells. Labour has not been in power for 18 years and it has not completely shed its old tax-and-spend image for some investors.

The latest projections from the BBC suggest Labour will secure a 183 seat majority in the 659-seat parliament, raising the prospect of two, maybe even three terms for the incoming government. This may be enough to make some investors recoil from gilts.

"The big fear is the size of the Labour majority," said Andy Cates, senior UK economist at UBS. "We think the left wing faction is likely to be very small, which will make it easier for Blair to pursue policies which he tried so hard to make the market believe are credible."
Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic advisor at Bank of America, said the size of the majority made Labour's first budget and monetary policy meeting crucial.

Analysts agreed incoming Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown would raise rates by at least 25 basis points at the next monetary meeting with Bank of England governor Eddie George, in a rush to reassure markets the economy is in safe hands.
That meeting is expected to go ahead on May 7 as scheduled, according to Peter Jay, the BBC's economics editor.

"This is very much a credibility issue now," said Hawkins. "I suspect gilts will open down a bit as people take stock and wonder if all the rhetoric and promises of Tony Blair hold water. But I think people will give him the benefit of the doubt."
Kleinwort's Scott said the more pro-European stance of New Labour would soon begin to give a boost to gilts.
He said before long, pro European Economic and Monetary Union rhetoric from the new government would filter down to underpin the British bond market.

Ten-year spreads with Bunds should narrow medium term, said analysts, although a slight shake-out immediate term could mean the gap balloons to 190 basis points or even 200. The spread was at 183 basis points around the close of trade on Thursday.
